strengths: The paper articulates a useful and important inductive bias for learned mesh simulators: separating topology-fixed incidence structure from metric/constitutive and dissipative components. This is well motivated by DEC, port-Hamiltonian systems, and structure-preserving numerical methods.

MeshFT-Net is simple and interpretable: hard-wiring signed incidence operators and learning SPD/PSD metric or damping blocks gives clear physical guarantees such as energy conservation/dissipation under the stated model and integrator assumptions.

The empirical diagnostics go beyond one-step error. The paper reports rollout error, energy drift, wave-speed error, canonical consistency, PDE residuals, equipartition, momentum variation, OOD shifts, ablations, and computational cost, which is much more informative than standard short-horizon MSE alone.

The results on analytic wave benchmarks are strong and consistent: MeshFT-Net has much lower long-horizon error and energy drift than MGN, HNN-style, FNO, GraphCON, and PI-MGN baselines in the reported settings.

The ablations are conceptually helpful: removing signed orientation, scrambling topology, learning J freely, or relaxing metric positivity generally damages stability or physical diagnostics, supporting the practical value of the proposed structure.
weaknesses: The central reduction theorem appears overclaimed. The assumptions (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and energy balance/passivity) do not convincingly imply the very specific signed-incidence wiring claimed. In particular, Lemma A.1 asserts that any local permutation-equivariant linear map reduces to a small basis with shared scalar weights, which is not generally true on irregular meshes, heterogeneous cell complexes, or when local geometric/type features are allowed.

The proof seems to conflate a strong assumed port-Hamiltonian-like incremental energy condition with deriving port-Hamiltonian structure. Assumption E already imposes a conservative/dissipative split and two-point monotonicity/skew conditions; Lemma A.3 then largely restates the standard skew/dissipative Jacobian decomposition. This weakens the claimed novelty of deriving the structure from minimal physical principles.

There is a technical gap in applying the incidence-wiring lemma to J(z): the J obtained in Lemma A.3 includes the skew part of the dissipative Jacobian, and it is not shown that this matrix separately satisfies the locality/permutation/orientation hypotheses needed for Lemma A.4. Thus the main theorem's conclusion about the conservative interconnection is not fully justified.

The theoretical claim is local and Jacobian-level, but the paper repeatedly uses it to motivate global architectural and physical claims. The manuscript does include a remark limiting the theorem, but the surrounding text still suggests broader equation-agnostic and topology-fixed conclusions than the proof supports.

The empirical scope is narrower than the claims. Most quantitative results are on linear or near-linear periodic wave systems where DEC/FEM incidence structure is exactly the right inductive bias. The nonlinear experiment is synthetic and generated from the same structural family, so it does not strongly test model mismatch.

The realistic The Well experiment is weakly evaluated: it appears to provide only qualitative snapshots for MeshFT-Net, without quantitative metrics or baseline comparisons. This is insufficient support for claims about realistic acoustic scattering data.

Baselines may be disadvantaged. MeshFT-Net has very strong built-in knowledge of the target operator and orders of magnitude fewer parameters, while the baselines are relatively generic and sometimes wrapped in integrators or penalties whose fairness is hard to assess. More competitive structure-preserving baselines from DEC/data-driven exterior calculus or learned Hodge-star methods would be important.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript. It says code and exact seeds/configurations are provided as anonymous supplementary files or will be released upon acceptance, but many experimental details are deferred to released code. The review cannot fully verify implementation choices, tuning parity, or baseline fidelity from the paper alone.

Limitations are not adequately discussed. The paper does not clearly delimit when the approach fails, e.g. non-Hamiltonian/non-passive systems, shocks/contact discontinuities, learned topology, nonlocal constitutive laws, strong boundary/source effects, or dynamics where state-dependent interconnection is essential.

The impact statement is generic and does not discuss potential misuse or failure modes of physics simulators, such as over-trusting stable but biased rollouts in safety-critical engineering contexts. No major ethical issue is apparent, but the treatment is superficial.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: learning mesh-based physical simulators with stronger conservation/stability guarantees than generic message-passing models.

The topology/metric separation is a sensible inductive bias, well connected to DEC and port-Hamiltonian discretizations, and the resulting MeshFT-Net architecture is simple and computationally attractive.

The empirical sections include several useful diagnostics beyond one-step error, including energy drift, dispersion, PDE residuals, momentum variation, OOD shifts, and ablations of topology/orientation/metric constraints.
The reported results on analytic wave benchmarks are strong for the proposed method, especially long-horizon energy behavior and data efficiency.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not convincing as stated. The proof appears to assume very strong incremental energy/passivity and local energy-coordinate conditions that already imply much of the skew/dissipative port-Hamiltonian split, so the claimed deduction from minimal physical principles is overstated.

The incidence-wiring result is underjustified. Lemma A.1/A.2 appear to rule out same-degree and other local equivariant interactions by a restrictive basis argument, but this does not generally follow for arbitrary meshes, heterogeneous cell types, vector-valued features, nonlinear local maps, or realistic permutation equivariance. The theorem therefore seems much narrower than the abstract and conclusions suggest.

There is a mismatch between the broad claims and the implemented model. The theorem allows local state-dependent incidence gains and nonlinear constitutive structure, but the experiments mostly use a quadratic, state-independent metric/interconnection setting tailored to linear wave-like systems. This weakens the claim of a general framework for mesh-based continuum physics.

The empirical validation is too narrow and partly circular. Most quantitative results are on analytic plane waves where the proposed architecture hard-codes the correct DEC/Hamiltonian structure. The strongest baselines are not clearly tuned or adapted comparably, and some comparisons appear unfavorable by design rather than demonstrating broad superiority.

The realistic Acoustic Scattering experiment is inadequately evaluated: the main paper provides qualitative snapshots but no clear quantitative comparison against baselines on this dataset. Claims about realistic datasets, low drift, and correct dispersion are therefore not sufficiently supported there.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Many important settings are deferred to released code, and the manuscript repeatedly says exact hyperparameters are in supplementary/code. For review, the paper should specify enough model, optimizer, training, substepping/CFL, baseline tuning, and dataset details to reproduce the main claims from the text.

Presentation is polished at a high level but imprecise technically. Important distinctions between global versus local port-Hamiltonian form, continuous-time vector fields versus discrete integrators, canonical versus mixed cochain packaging, and learned versus fixed metric blocks are easy to miss and sometimes blur the actual contribution.

The limitations and impact discussion are superficial. The paper does not seriously discuss failure cases such as systems with nonlocal effects, advection/shocks, contact, topology changes, non-Hamiltonian forcing, boundary/source handling, or when the topology-fixed bias is too restrictive.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The architecture largely combines known ideas from DEC, structure-preserving discretization, port-Hamiltonian systems, and learned Hodge/constitutive operators; the claimed novelty rests on a reduction theorem whose assumptions and proof do not currently justify the broad framing.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and appealing inductive bias for mesh-based physical learning: fix the signed-incidence/topological interconnection and learn only metric/constitutive and dissipative factors. This is well motivated by DEC and port-Hamiltonian structure, and the architectural consequences are easy to understand.

The empirical results are broad for the main target setting. MeshFT-Net performs very strongly on analytic wave benchmarks, damped waves, physical-consistency diagnostics, OOD frequency/resolution/wave-speed shifts, and ablations. The ablations are especially useful because they directly test topology, orientation, metric positivity, and learned-vs-fixed interconnection choices.

The method gives excellent long-horizon stability and physical fidelity despite low parameter counts and modest computation. Tables on energy drift, momentum conservation, PDE residuals, and computational cost support the claim that the structural constraints improve rollout behavior beyond one-step error.
Presentation is generally strong. The paper explains the topology/metric separation well, connects the theorem to the network design, and includes substantial experimental details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical reduction appears stronger than what is fully justified. The proof of the incidence-wiring theorem relies on restrictive symmetry/locality arguments, and it is not obvious that the stated assumptions rule out all same-degree or more general local couplings in realistic heterogeneous meshes. The step from orientation covariance and passivity to the specific diagonal positive incidence gain structure seems under-argued.

The theorem is local and Jacobian-level, while some parts of the paper's narrative imply a broader dynamical or global port-Hamiltonian characterization. The manuscript does include a remark limiting the claim, but the framing still risks overclaiming what the result establishes.

Most quantitative evidence is on systems very close to the proposed inductive bias, especially linear wave-like dynamics with known incidence structure. The realistic The Well acoustic experiment is mainly qualitative in the main paper and lacks quantitative baselines, so evidence for impact beyond matched wave settings is weaker.

The comparison to baselines is useful but not always fully satisfying. Some baselines are structurally disadvantaged for long-horizon conservation, and details such as tuning effort, integrator choices, and fairness of damping/metric parameterizations are partly deferred to released code rather than being completely self-contained.

Limitations and ethics are treated lightly. The paper would benefit from a more explicit limitations section discussing when topology-fixed interconnections are inappropriate, how boundary/source terms and nonlinear state-dependent interconnections scale, and failure modes under model mismatch.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete from the manuscript alone: code is promised or supplied as anonymous supplementary material, while several exact hyperparameters and implementation details are delegated to the released code. This is acceptable if the supplement is complete, but the paper itself is not fully standalone.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: stable, physically faithful learned simulators on meshes. The topology/metric separation is a useful and well-motivated design principle, connecting DEC, port-Hamiltonian systems, and mesh neural simulators in a coherent way.

MeshFT-Net is a plausible and practically attractive architecture: fixing signed-incidence conservative couplings while learning SPD/PSD metric and dissipation factors gives a clear inductive bias, low parameter count, and favorable computational cost.

The empirical section is broad. The paper evaluates analytic waves, dissipative dynamics, OOD shifts, irregular heterogeneous elasticity, nonlinear lattice systems, ablations, and runtime/memory scaling. Many results show strong long-horizon stability and conservation advantages over MGN, HNN, FNO, GraphCON, and related variants.

The ablations are especially useful: breaking orientation/topology or metric positivity often preserves one-step error while destroying long-horizon physical behavior, which supports the architectural choices even if the theorem is not fully convincing.
Presentation is generally clear, with helpful notation, algorithmic detail, and appendix descriptions of datasets, metrics, and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The main theoretical claim appears overstated and not fully sound as written. The proof that locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and energy balance force signed-incidence port-Hamiltonian wiring relies on strong and sometimes unclear assumptions. For example, Lemma B.1 treats permutation equivariance as forcing only identity/adjacency/incidence basis terms with shared scalar weights, but this is not generally true on irregular meshes with geometry/material features, heterogeneous local neighborhoods, or equivariance only under mesh relabelings rather than arbitrary degree-wise permutations.

The orientation-covariance argument is under-specified. The manuscript mixes orientation gauge transformations of cochains with transformations of the incidence matrices, and statements such as single-degree flips changing signs of D need a more careful treatment for arbitrary cell-wise orientation changes. As a result, the step ruling out same-degree local terms and deriving only incidence cross-degree coupling is not convincing in full generality.

The energy/passivity assumption is stronger than advertised. The theorem assumes a conservative/dissipative split and an incremental two-point energy condition, which is close to assuming the skew/dissipative Jacobian structure needed for the port-Hamiltonian representation. This weakens the claim that the structure is deduced from minimal physical principles.

There is a gap between the theorem and the implemented model. The theorem is local and Jacobian-level, permits state-dependent incidence gains, and assumes a local energy reparameterization; most experiments use a quadratic/state-independent metric and fixed normalized J. The paper would benefit from a more explicit statement that the architecture is a restricted heuristic instantiation rather than a direct consequence of the full theorem.

The realistic-data evidence is weaker than the synthetic evidence. The Well acoustic scattering experiment is mainly qualitative in the main text, without comparable quantitative baselines, so claims about realistic datasets are less strongly supported than the analytic and controlled nonlinear benchmarks.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The appendix gives many hyperparameters and data-generation details, but repeatedly defers exact settings to released code; the abstract says code is available but the visible manuscript does not provide a usable link. Some baseline fairness details remain unclear, especially where MeshFT receives structure-specific variables, substepping/CFL guards, damping operators, or theory Hodge information that baselines may not receive equivalently.

Several baselines appear pedagogical rather than strongest possible. More competitive structure-preserving DEC/FEM, port-Hamiltonian, symplectic, or neural-operator baselines tailored to these PDE classes would make the empirical significance clearer.

The paper does not include a substantive limitations or ethics discussion. Risks of overinterpreting benchmark-specific conservation diagnostics, benchmark leakage/contamination, failure on non-Hamiltonian or nonlocal physics, and misuse in safety-critical simulation are not concretely discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: building mesh-based learned simulators that preserve topological structure, energy behavior, and long-horizon stability. The DEC/port-Hamiltonian framing is a sensible and potentially useful inductive bias.

The architecture is clearly motivated at a high level: fix signed-incidence structure and learn metric/constitutive/dissipative terms. This separation is physically meaningful for several PDE families and could be valuable in practice.

The experiments include several useful diagnostics beyond one-step MSE, including energy drift, PDE residuals, dispersion-related metrics, momentum variation, OOD resolution/frequency/parameter shifts, and ablations of topology/metric/orientation structure.

The reported results, if reproduced, suggest that the proposed structured model can be very data-efficient and stable on wave-like systems where the assumed topology-metric separation matches the data-generating process.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not sufficiently convincing. The theorem is presented as deriving port-Hamiltonian incidence wiring from broad principles, but the proof relies on strong and partly hidden assumptions: a local energy coordinate already exists, the dynamics are split into conservative and dissipative components satisfying incremental passivity conditions, and the Jacobian-level map is constrained by a simplified linear local basis. These assumptions are close to the desired conclusion and substantially weaken the claimed derivation.

The locality/permutation-equivariance argument appears too strong for realistic meshes. Lemma B.1 effectively reduces any local equivariant linear operator to identity, adjacency, and incidence terms with shared scalar weights, but irregular meshes with geometry/material features permit many local equivariant operators not captured by this basis. The proof also does not adequately justify the positive diagonal incidence gains beyond an orientation gauge argument.

There is a serious mismatch between the theorem and much of the experimental implementation. The main theorem is formulated for adjacent cochain pairs with off-diagonal signed-incidence blocks, but Appendix D says the experiments often use canonical variables z=(q,p) with canonical symplectic J and K=D^T W D absorbed into the metric. This makes it unclear whether the empirical model is actually an instantiation of the claimed local reduction or a conventional structured wave solver with learned Hodge-like weights.

The empirical comparison is not fully persuasive. The analytic plane-wave tasks strongly favor the proposed inductive bias, while the baselines appear pedagogical rather than competitive. There is no strong comparison to classical DEC/FEM structure-preserving solvers, learned Hodge-star methods, or better-tuned port-Hamiltonian/neural operator variants. Several baselines diverge by large margins, raising concerns about implementation or tuning fairness.

The acoustic-scattering section is weakly supported. It is presented as validation on realistic data, but the main text provides mostly qualitative snapshots and vague statements rather than a complete quantitative comparison, despite making claims about low drift and correct dispersion.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. The abstract says code is available but the provided line appears blank in the manuscript. Many exact hyperparameters and implementation details are deferred to the released code, which is not actually specified in the paper text. Several tables report only 3 seeds, and important evaluation choices, CFL substepping, architecture capacities, and baseline tuning details are insufficiently documented.

The paper lacks an explicit limitations and ethics discussion. Important limitations are not clearly acknowledged, including restriction to systems compatible with the fixed topology-metric split, possible failure under nonlocal physics/contact/advection-dominated flows, dependence on known mesh incidence structure, and the gap between Jacobian-level local statements and global rollout behavior.

Presentation is uneven. The manuscript contains notation inconsistencies such as G versus G^{-1}/mass maps, grammatical errors, and overclaiming language. The contribution would be easier to assess if the theorem assumptions, implementation choices, and experimental instantiations were separated more carefully.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful inductive bias for mesh-based learned simulators: fix signed-incidence/topological conservative structure and learn metric/constitutive/dissipative factors. This is well motivated by DEC and port-Hamiltonian structure, and the architecture follows naturally from the thesis.

The empirical evaluation is broad and generally convincing: analytic plane waves, dissipative dynamics, physical-consistency diagnostics, OOD frequency/resolution/wave-speed shifts, irregular heterogeneous elasticity, nonlinear lattice systems, ablations, and computational-cost measurements. MeshFT-Net consistently improves long-horizon stability, energy behavior, momentum preservation, and data efficiency.

The ablations are a major strength. The topology-metric separation, orientation/topology/metric violations, and state-dependent coupling experiments directly test the paper's central modeling claims rather than only reporting prediction error.

Presentation is mostly clear, with helpful notation, a concrete coboundary example, and detailed appendix descriptions of data generation, metrics, and training setups. The work is potentially significant for structure-preserving learned simulation on meshes.
weaknesses: The theoretical reduction appears overstated. The proof relies on strong and somewhat informal assumptions, especially the local/permutation-equivariant linear basis argument and the claim that orientation covariance rules out all same-degree terms. On irregular meshes with geometry/material features, arbitrary relabeling, local heterogeneity, and possible skew same-degree couplings, the uniqueness of signed-incidence wiring is not fully established.

The energy/passivity assumption is very strong: the incremental two-point condition essentially imposes the skew/dissipative Jacobian split the theorem later derives. This weakens the sense in which the port-Hamiltonian form is discovered from minimal principles.

Several empirical comparisons may favor the proposed method structurally. Baselines are described as pedagogically clear rather than highly optimized, and many experiments use systems generated by incidence-based dynamics, so the inductive bias is very well matched. Stronger comparisons to mature geometric/structure-preserving discretization-learning methods would improve confidence.

The acoustic scattering experiment is mostly qualitative and appears to lack quantitative comparison to baselines, despite being the main realistic-data claim. This limits the evidence that the method transfers beyond controlled synthetic settings.

Reproducibility is only partially adequate. The paper repeatedly says exact hyperparameters are in the released code, but the code link in the extracted manuscript is blank. Some main-text tables omit standard deviations, and important details are deferred to unreleased code.

The limitations and ethics treatment is thin. There is a generic impact statement but no substantive limitations section discussing restricted state-independent interconnection assumptions, possible failures on non-Hamiltonian/dissipative systems, boundary/source handling, or domains where topology-fixed structure is inappropriate.
